4 Incidental Trainers
1.2 WHO ARE “INCIDENTAL TRAINERS”?
You may be one of them! If you are a professional in any field, at some point in your
career or business you probably will be training employees or clients, making you
an incidental trainer.
The term “incidental trainers” used in this book refers to professionals who have
training as an incidental responsibility in their job or business. Most often they are
not full-time trainers. They are subject-matter experts in diverse professions, such
as engineering, law, safety, marketing, research, health care, risk ­management,
­information technology, and many others. Since they have the technical expertise,
it is assumed that they can teach others on the subject matter. The safety manager
at the audited facility mentioned above is one of them. His expertise is in health
and safety in the workplace, not in training or adult education. Since he is the
safety ­manager, however, safety training naturally falls in his lap. Other examples
abound in almost every professional field and every organization. For instance, an
­experienced ­engineer may have the additional duty of providing on-the-job ­training
to a new engineer, or a sales manager may need to train a team of sales representa­
tives. Outside of the employment relationship, consultants and other business ­persons
­frequently assume the role of incidental trainers. A technology consultant may teach
clients how to maximize the benefits from certain computer software; a communica­
tions expert may train his clients on how to use a newly installed telephone system.
The training may be in a group setting or one-to-one.
1.3 WIIFY—WHAT’S IN IT FOR YOU?
In your responsibility as an incidental trainer, what happens if the training does not
go well? It diminishes your credibility as a subject-matter expert. No matter how
knowledgeable and experienced you are in the field, your trainees will not appreciate
your expertise if they feel that they have not learned anything from your training. It
could reflect poorly on your performance even though “training” may not have been
specified in your job description!
How can you ensure the effectiveness of your training to satisfy your employers,
clients, or trainees? Effective training:
Remediates deficiencies
Educates and entertains trainees
Stimulates higher performance
Uses skilled instructors
Lengthens retention time
Tests competencies
Supports organizational goals
In other words, effective training produces RESULTS.
This book will guide you through the process of training design, development, and
delivery to help you achieve effectiveness in your training program. Since this book
is written with the incidental trainer in mind, it emphasizes practical techniques that

Introduction 5
you can put to use easily. Incidental trainers typically spend less than half of their
time in training and must manage that time wisely.
Part 1 of this book, “Fundamentals of Training,” presents a step-by-step guide
from training design to program validation. Part 2, “Training, Like the Pros,” delves
into specific topics and discusses best practices to help you enhance your training
effectiveness to match those of professional trainers. At the same time, even full-
time trainers may pick up new ideas that help them be more successful!
1.4 WHAT ARE THE SEVEN KEYS TO SUCCESSFUL TRAINING?
To be a successful trainer, you must first remember what training is all about. The
Merriam-Webster Online (2011) defines “training” as “the act, process, or method of
one that trains” and “the skill, knowledge, or experience acquired by one that trains.”
These definitions use the word “trains” from the perspectives of a trainer and a
trainee. They imply that training is a process whereby the trainer imparts knowledge
and skills to the trainee. Within the business world, another characteristic of training
is that it must be supportive of an organization’s goals. Hence, this book adopts the
following definition:
Training is a communication process involving interaction between trainer and
trainee, the purpose of which is to transfer knowledge, teach skills, or ­transform
behavior in support of the achievement of an organization’s goals.
Note that the literature sometimes refers to changing “attitude” rather than “­behavior.”
For example, Brethower (2000, 490) states that knowledge, skills, and attitudes are
the “traditional domain of instructional content.” Bloom’s taxonomy (1956, 12), as
explained in Chapter 4, defines learner behaviors to include ways in which learners
think or feel. Also, feelings are not directly observable and must be measured by
behavioral indicators. For these reasons, the term “behavior” is used in the above
definition of training.
Is training different from teaching? Both training and teaching offer the
­learners an educational experience. As Smith and Ragan (2005, 5) state, training
is ­distinguished from teaching in that the former focuses on skills that learners can
immediately apply to improve job competency, whereas the latter targets skills of
a more general nature that are not directed toward specific job tasks. Due to the
­similarity, instructional design techniques in teaching are applicable to training and
vice versa. Due to the difference, one of the critical success factors in training is
unique, and that is organizational support for the training program.
The seven keys to success of a training program are:
1. Organizational support
2. Needs assessment
3. Training plan
4. Competency assessment
5. Presentation and facilitation
6. Course evaluation
7. Program validation

6 Incidental Trainers
These critical success factors apply whether you are providing training within your
own organization or for your clients. By the same token, discussions in this book that
make reference to “employee” are equally applicable whether the ­employees are your
organization’s employees or your clients or their employees.
While a validated training program helps to garner more organizational support,
obtaining organizational support requires business management skills more than
training skills. For this reason, the topic of organizational support is deferred to
Part 2. The next chapter begins by looking at two types of needs assessment, both of
which are necessary to determine if and what kind of training is desirable and how
best to set the goals of the training.
REFERENCES

Goals; Book 1 Cognitive Domain. New York: Longman.

Creating and Delivering Training Programs—Instructor-Led, Computer-Based, or Self-
Directed, edited by G. M. Piskurich, P. Beckschi, and B. Hall. New York: McGraw-Hill,
pp. 473–491.

webster.com/dictionary/training.
Smith, P. L., and T. J. Ragan. 2005. Instructional Design. 3rd ed. Hoboken: Wiley/
Jossey-Bass Education.

rooms. In this study, the objective was to describe the inci-
dence and characteristics of emergency room (ER) visits
associated with unintentional falls in the United States.
Methods: The authors performed a secondary analysis on
data from the National Center for Health Statistics National
Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey for 1992–1994.
An ER visit was defined as fall-related if an ICD-9-CM
cause of injury code was reported as E880.0-886.9 or E888.
Results: There were an estimated 7,946,000 fall-related
ER visits per year, corresponding to an annual rate of 3.1
per 100 persons (95% CI = 2.8 to 3.4). Children under 5
years of age, comprised the largest proportion of visits
(14%). Among those visits, coded with respect to place of
occurrence, the rate of visits, associated with falls, occur-
ring at home (1.7/100; 95% CI = 1.6 to 1.9) was signifi-
cantly higher, than that associated with falls, occurring in all
other locations combined (1.1/100; 95% CI = 1.0 to 1.2).
The mean injury-severity score increased significantly with
the age of the patient. Fall-related ER visits resulted in an
estimated 860,000 hospitalizations, 62 percent of which
involved individuals aged 65 years and older. An estimated
$2.45 billion per year was paid for fall-related ER visits. Gov-
ernment sources paid all or part of 41 percent of visits.
Conclusions: This study reports nationally representa-
tive data describing the incidence and characteristics of fall-
related ER visits. These data expand what is known about
the epidemiology of falls and help to define the burden that
fall injuries place on ERs in the United States. The results of
this study could serve as a benchmark to evaluate the effec-
tiveness of future fall prevention efforts.
Courtesy the Academy of Emergency Medicine. For updates and further
information, refer to www.Medscape.com.

another type of arrangement became prevalent in the telegraph industry for pole
climbers. Surprisingly, much of the advice on the utility industry lineman’s belt care
and maintenance offered in a 1928 textbook still is valid today.
Safety devices that were designed to be passive, until a fall occurred, began to
develop in the early part of the twentieth century. Perhaps, because of photographs
and publicity from investigations following accidents, high-rise window cleaners
were the first to take an interest in independent lifelines. Between World Wars I
and II, several manufacturers of body belts and other fall protection equipment
emerged.
The first retracting lifelines were introduced in Sweden after World War II for
mining applications. Around the same time, the first climbing protection devices
that required no manipulation were developed; the U.S. Navy and Federal Aviation
Administration (FAA) immediately began using them for tower climbing.
In 1952 the National Safety Council (NSC), and the American Society of Safety
Engineers (ASSE) published a report on maximum arrest force, based upon rapid
deceleration tests of cadavers and anesthetized dogs. Later, these findings helped
to lay the foundation for Japan’s 1,800-pound fall protection equipment force limit.
In 1967, the Boeing Company published a test report (Report No. 2-1886-09)
demonstrating the superiority of harnesses and energy-absorber lanyards over
belts and ropes.
Ladder-safety devices began to be widely recognized in the 1950s and 1960s.
And during the 1960s and 1970s, the availability and characteristics of synthetic
fibers caused a shift away from the natural fibers used in lifelines and from the
leather used in belts. Parachute-style harnesses became popular for emergency
retrieval through narrow top openings of confined spaces.
Research in Europe showed the use of a full-body harness was a necessity for
fall protection because of superior support, both during and after a fall arrest.
Equipment standards were developed in the 1970s in many countries based upon
widespread research into force levels on the body.
Fall-hazard tolerance, by employers in the United States, was on a plateau
in the 1970s and 1980s. The American National Standards Institute (ANSI)
guideline A10.14-1975, and other A10 standards, reflected industry practice, where
anchorage points were natural and convenient; “tying off” was the answer in these
cases. Otherwise, no protection became a logical conclusion. ANSI A10.14-1975
was retired in 1987 under the ANSI sunset rule. The A10.32 became the successor
to the A10.14 and was finished in 1997 but held as the committee sponsorship
changed from the National Safety Council (NSC) to the American Society of
Safety Engineers (ASSE); it was finally was published in 2004.
The Z359 committee was granted the right to form in 1987 by ANSI under
the ASSE secretariat and with great support from industry, and a number of
construction companies, it issued its first standard in 1992 for personal fall arrest.
It took another 15 years to develop what has become known as the Fall Protection
Code. This set of standards began to be issued in 2007 and includes the Z359.2
standard “Comprehensive Managed Fall Protection Programs,” which gives
guidance on titles of responsibility and minimum training requirements.
10 • Introduction

1989, 1995, 2003, and 2009. In the 1980s, confined space standards in many states
merely required an attendant-tending rope for rescue. The revised ANSI Z117.1
standard requires wearing fall arrest equipment before entry, if practical, and helps
define the criteria for fall protection and retrieval through training. Beyond the
OSHA 1910.146 standard, it is the intention of OSHA is to issue a construction
standard for confined spaces, the A10.43 draft Confined Space Standard for
construction, and now the NFPA1006-2008 Confined Space Rescue Standard
Committee may make following the rules more complex in the future.
As a result of divisions in thinking, a free-standing ANSI Committee, ANSI
Z359, sponsored by the American Society of Safety Engineers (ASSE), was
established to address fall protection for all industry areas, except construction and
demolition. The charter and standing of the American National Standards Z359
Committee on Standards for Fall Protection was accredited by ANSI on January 6,
1988. Its goal was to create a standards matrix to cover systems, anchorages, and
testing for the following: (1) fall arrest; (2) work positioning; and (3) rescue and
evacuation. The first standard, Z359.1-1992 (reaffirmed 1999), covered fall arrest
systems and did not permit the use of body belts for fall arrest. The Z359.1-1992
was the most advanced free-standing, general industrystandard, at the time. The
Z359-2007 set of standards, dubbed The Fall Protection Code, continued that advance.
Up to 18 fall protection standards are being developed as the Z359 Code has been
unbundled into component and engineering standards, allowing for more timely
introductions and improved opportunities for updates.
History of the ANSI Fall Protection Standards
The need for fall protection standards activity grew out of several preexisting
conditions. Between 1970 and 1980, fall protection equipment and methods
advanced beyond the coverage of the U.S. standards and government regulations
published up to that time. That trend continued through the 1980s. Reform of fall
protection standards in industrialized nations throughout the world, and drafting
of a new international standard, got under way early in that decade. In 1983, the
United States joined the ISO effort on fall protection.
At the same time, the pertinent construction industry standards were due for
revision. There were a few specialized standards that addressed specific industries
or specific equipment and techniques. However, there were no broadly applicable
U.S. standards for much of the equipment, and the methods in commonplace
industrial use, or for occupational or non-occupational fall protection. A task force
of the ANSI Safety and Health Standards Board recommended formation of a
free-standing committee to address the subject of fall protection. The ANSI’s
TAG, which represents the U.S. fall protection interests to the ISO, acted upon the
Safety and Health Standards Board recommendation and initiated formation of
the Z359 Committee. The ASSE assumed the Secretariat.
Historically, the notions of user positioning, fall prevention, restraint, and
fall arrest have been mingled in the literature; as a result, their distinguishing
characteristics have not been agreed upon. However, the requirements imposed on

lines for process control away from the reach of heavy-duty forklifts puts battery
replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff
and cave rescue, as well as from mountaineering techniques. In the middle 1800s,
Introduction to Fall Protection • 9

Collapse of Work Surfaces
Collapse of work surfaces is usually found on construction sites, scaffolds, and
roofs due to insufficiently unsupported surfaces and renovation projects, due to
floor-material degradation or towers and antennas and corrosion, for example.
Before a worker walks on a work surface, such as a commercial roof or metal
decking, an engineer should have periodically reviewed the condition of the
structure and deemed it fit for use (OSHA 1926.501(a)(2)). This review can be done
from aerial lifts or crane-suspended work platforms, for evaluation of ladders and
platforms. Alternatively, subfloors can be observed from the floor below. When in
doubt, avoid human access, or consider grating or plywood working surfaces for
temporary use.
Trips: Falls on the Same Level
A trip is defined as a loss of balance due to the foot (or leg) contacting an object,
or obstruction, when the attention is directed to the path ahead. A slight increase
or decrease in the walking surface of one-quarter inch (6.35 mm) is often sufficient
to cause a stumble (trip), resulting in loss of balance. On occasion, too much
friction between the foot or footwear and the walking surface also can cause a trip,
especially when moving from one type of surface to another. Unsecured throw
rugs or raised door thresholds, result in tripping hazards in the home can also
cause problems; seniors would do well to put favorite rugs on the wall instead of
the floor.
Broken sign stubs on sidewalks or other walking areas need to be dealt with
immediately because pedestrians cannot easily see these kinds of tripping hazards,
and a severe fall can occur. Especially troublesome are shoelaces that can catch on
the obstruction and fling the person headfirst into the ground or another object.
Shoelace loops from one shoe can catch on the other shoe’s lacing hooks, resulting
in an abrupt fall, with a likely head injury. Another common problem is stepping
on loose shoelaces from the other shoe, which can produce a stumble.
Stumbles
A stumble is the loss of contact with a surface while walking or stepping up or
down, which may or may not result in a fall. A forward stumble could be the result
of an unexpected change in elevation, as when stepping off from an unusually
high curb for example. Stumbles backward can result from a sudden change in
elevation, such as an unobserved roof blister, next to an unguarded roof edge.
This can produce an involuntary backwards stumble that could be catastrophic.
Housekeeping
Poor or inadequate housekeeping, such as blocked aisles, exposed cords, and
uneven rugs, mats, or runners, are a few conditions that often produce trips.
A poor physical layout can promote dangerous shortcuts. The emotional state
16 • Introduction

include transportation and public utilities, forestry, mining, agriculture, fishing,
wholesale and retail trades, and services.
In 2006, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that fatal work injuries
involving falls increased 5 percent in 2006, after a sharp decrease in 2005. The 827
fatal falls in 2006 was the highest total since 1992, when the fatality census began.
Fatal falls from roofs increased from 160 fatalities in 2005 to 184 in 2006, a rise of
15 percent. Falls from ladders (16%), scaffolds (11%) and roofs (23%), still account
for the majority of falls. Identifying fall hazards and deciding how best to protect
workers is the first step in reducing or eliminating fall hazards. BLS reported a
decrease in fall deaths during 2008 and 2009. In 2009, BLS data indicated that
the number of fatal falls was down to a total of 645. BLS further surmised that
the decrease in fall deaths might have been a reflection of the decline in overall
construction activity, as construction accidents typically account for over half of
all fatal falls (BLS 2011). The U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) lists falls as one
of the leading causes of traumatic occupational death, accounting for 8 percent
of all occupational fatalities from trauma (DOL/BLS 2010). Any time a worker
is at a height of 4 feet or more, the worker is at risk and needs to be protected.
Fall protection must be provided at 4 feet trigger height in general industry,
5 feet in maritime, and 6 feet, generally, in construction. However, regardless of
the fall distance, fall protection must be provided when working over dangerous
equipment and machinery and in aerial lifts.
Has Fall Protection Been Available to and Used by Elevated Fall Victims?
In a unique 1984 BLS study, “Injuries Resulting from Falls from Elevation,”
10 percent of fall victims surveyed had been provided with fall arrest systems;
however, more than 75 percent were not attached to a lifeline or structure. The
majority of these workers reported, that they were unwilling or unable to connect
their body support because they were moving around. A few stated that there was
no place to connect their equipment. Sixteen workers were using fall protection
equipment at the time of their elevated falls. For 10 of these workers, the fall
protection consisted of a belt, attached with a lanyard, yet four sustained back
injuries from the fall arrest. That small sample of work-related incidents clearly
indicated that too many workers in American industry are not only injured or
killed, falling from one level to another, but a substantial number of falls resulted
from a failure to properly use and attach the fall arrest equipment.
BLS statistics tell us that from 1992 to 1999, fatal falls accounted for 10–11% of
all fatal work injuries, increasing to 12–14% during 2000–2006 (DOL/BLS 2008).
This suggests strongly that similar usage failures, despite great strides in training,
regulations, standards, and equipment, remain. This problem is not isolated within
one industry or one work task. Either fall protection is still not being adequately
provided or the equipment that is provided is being used or applied improperly.
22 • Introduction

We can plan safety at heights, and we can train employees in better work
methods, but too many supervisors still leave the entire choice of work method
and safety provisions to the worker. “After all, he chose this line of work, and has
the job experience, so he should know best,” goes the reasoning, along with “I
can’t be with the worker, and do her job for her.”
Workers often play into this rationale by saying the boss said he will get me
anything I want for safety. While that is nice, the worker does not know what to
ask for, so the hazard exposures remain.
Too often, the necessary tools for safety have not been provided to the worker.
Tolerating fall hazards has become an unconsciously accepted practice many
managers develop early in their careers. The critical safety knowledge needed to
deal with heights safely is not inherent in the minds of most managers. It must be
learned. They unfortunately think that workers who fall were not careful enough
or simply were unlucky. “Poor Joe, what a shame,” is the refrain.
Prevention or Fall Arrest as a Means of Fall Protection?
Sometimes, exposure to a fall hazard cannot be practically prevented during access
to a work task or when at a work position, through such measures as floors, walls,
aerial lifts, bucket trucks, guardrails, perimeter cables, crane-suspended work
platforms (manbaskets), scaffolds, or planking. In these situations, personal fall
arrest equipment can be selected to control a fall or alternatively provide a reliable
means of escape when a controlled-descent feature is employed.
In general, personal protective equipment is designed as a backup safety system
for an individual during a work task. In the event of an emergency, the equipment
should function automatically to help protect the worker from harm. A personal-fall
protection system should, therefore, provide continuous and complete protection
without interfering with required task mobility. Continuous fall protection uses
one or more of the following means:
• Fall Prevention
Barriers, Covers
Guardrails
Perimeter Cables
Walls, Fences
Platforms, Buckets, Aerial Lifts
Scaffolds, Planking
• Fall Arrest
Safety Nets
Personal Fall Arrest Systems
Continuous or 100% fall protection means no gaps in fall protection coverage.
Many ask whether this can be done on an economical or practical basis. Properly
used, equipment can often provide the most protection for the least cost with a
certain level of potential exposure.

Preface to the Fourth Edition
The fall-protection revolution has begun! Maybe it was the harness rule in the
United States on January 1, 1998, when harnesses became a requirement and body
belts became illegal for fall arrest. It took only about a year for almost complete
compliance—not only in construction but also in general industry and other
industries. The word got around fast that suspension in a belt was dangerous.
So why is the number and rate of fatal falls still steadily going up? I think there are
two reasons: First, the proper structural anchorage point has not caught on widely
yet (beyond the standard issue of a harness and Y-lanyard). Second, the users of
fall-protection systems do not understand that these systems must be engineered
into the workplace and also maintained with strong, effective programs that
resemble FAA requirements for maintenance of commercial aircraft components.
The program administrator recommended in ANSI Z359.2 can help establish a
stronger role for the Qualified Person and more discipline for the Competent
Person. Advisory standards must begin to focus on incorporation of elements into
the building codes to provide designers with a set of requirements so new buildings
are not immediately in violation of OSHA requirements when the certificate of
occupancy or equivalent is provided.
The Competent Person can help prevent or repair damage that is caused by others
inadvertently and deal with innocent misuse. And as more sophisticated equipment
gets more widely used, there is the tendency to forego critical observations of
how the equipment is actually being used. Supervisors who fail to frequently
monitor work practices, inspect equipment, and check site conditions do so at the
risk of exposing workers to swing falls, cable cutting hazards, rope degradation
under acid conditions, edge hazards, corrosion of cable terminations, SRL pawl
sticking, ground or surface impacts, Y-lanyard deployment hazards, and snaphook
attachment hazards, just to name a few.
This book provides multiple solutions to eliminate fall hazards in more than one
trade or situation and tools to improve fall-hazard observations and documentation.
Recommendations herein for personal training for the exposed worker are vitally
important to reduce exposure to falls, but so too are the many recommendations
for designing out fall hazards and providing engineered anchorages for those who
must maintain buildings long after they are built.
As we march down the road of progress with improved equipment and systems and
standards, let us not forget the importance of the skill of recognizing fall hazards.
Certain exposures, even for a few milliseconds of duration, such as during transitions,
xii • Preface to the Fourth Edition

are potentially lethal and must be addressed by proper training. Even the best
harness with slack webbing adjustment controls and convenient buckle tightening
cannot make up for a poor application or excess fall exposure or nonattachment.
J. Nigel Ellis, Ph.D., PE, CSP, CPE
Introduction to Fall Protection • xiii

Are There Fall Hazards in Every Industry?
Nearly every industry, at some time, engages in work at elevation. The job could
range from the simple use of a 10-foot stepladder to change a light bulb to operating
a powered platform 185 feet up inside a boiler or climbing 200 feet up a flare-stack
ladder. A short, but unique, six-month Bureau of Labor Statistics study (1984)
of approximately 77 elevated-fall injuries showed a variety of industries were
involved. Although injuries in the construction industry were predominant in this
survey (41%), nearly one-fourth of the victims were employed by manufacturers.
Forty-four percent of the injured workers were craft workers, including carpenters
(10%) and mechanics/repairers (6%). A large portion, 24 percent, were working
as laborers, while 12 percent were employed as operators. Other victims included
clerical and sales workers, managers, and transport equipment operators. The
author has found that annually, over the past three decades, the relative numbers
change very little, and surveys may be unique such as this one.
Certain industries, of course, require substantial elevated work. For instance,
frequent elevated tasks associated with transmission and distribution operations in
the utility industry are significantly different from operations within a microchip
processing plant. For those industries, with frequent activity at elevation, the
probability of a fall is consequently higher. In some industries, such as trucking,
the access problems to tank trucks, flatbeds, and soft sides, have hardly begun to
be observed.
There are two types of elevated fall exposure:
1. During Work. Elevated work can be an integral part of a job or trade.
Scalers, for example, whose job it is to remove built-up residue from tanks,
digesters, or vessels, are often exposed to fall hazards, slipping, and chemicals
on an ongoing basis. Other examples, often associated with construction or
maintenance, include roofing, painting, sandblasting, pipe welding, masonry,
or bricklaying, and utility service work. Steel connectors also commonly
work at great elevation.
2. During Access or Exit. In other cases, exposure to a fall hazard occurs
simply while the worker is accessing an elevated workstation. Repair of a
valve, located on the upper tier of a chemical processing pipe rack, may
require that the worker use a fixed ladder 25 to 100 yards away, then walk
the pipe to the valve. Some trades, such as scaffold builders, provide a local
means of access. However, fall protection for these workers, during erection
and dismantling, should not be ignored. Temporary systems can be brought
to the site and removed by the contract scaffold company. Alternatively,
fall protection for access can be provided by the principal/owner and used
throughout the job by other employees.
Access to work areas can provide the greatest hazards, depending upon the
access method selected. Use of a rental van roof to paint signs on an automobile
dealership window is novel but raises questions. Use of a six-foot stepladder, next
to or within a few feet of a guardrail, raises the danger stakes. Running computer
8 • Introduction

lines for process control away from the reach of heavy-duty forklifts puts battery
replacement service 10 feet overhead next to a column. Planning and coordination
is a must for access for repeat visits and especially for single visits. Wiring for the
internet and telecommunications has made utility access a significant hazard above
almost every corridor when old wires are not replaced and new wires follow no
plan for their location.
Often, contractors are brought in to perform elevated work. It could be a
maintenance contract that requires the contractor to climb unprotected towers
and stacks to change aviation warning lights after a letter from the FAA is received
or a complete repair project involving a number of crews. It is still not unusual
to hear a company executive respond, “Oh, we don’t send our people up there—
we contract that out!” This means elevated tasks at a particular worksite can be
accomplished, provided the contractor’s employees are well trained, well equipped,
and guided by solid requirements in the bid document and contractor rulebook
to provide fall protection followed by the necessary site-specific training. This is
especially important to the owner because of third-party legal relationships, which
are not easily appreciated. Therefore, a workable system for establishing and
checking procedures and then observing for compliance is critical and may involve
a local safety consultant to review work if no qualified maintenance person or
safety professional is available.
Falls, caused by slipping or tripping, can lead to more serious elevated falls and
must be addressed (see Chapter 4).
Public fall exposure at elevation is presented primarily by stairs and a myriad of
railing designs, followed by ladders, roofs, and walking close to construction sites.
Tree stands pose a major fall threat to 30 million hunters, which is of particular
interest to employers, who expect their hunter- workers to show up on Mondays
during the hunting season.
Fall Protection from a Historical Perspective
“When one falls, it is not one’s foot that is to blame.”—Chinese proverb
For thousands of years, people have used ropes and various knots to help
move or secure objects against the forces of gravity. Bend knots were used to
gain a reliable hold, and hitch knots were used in moving a load by sliding along
another rope and, if necessary, gripping to lock the load in place. The practice of
people climbing ladders and/or being suspended on ropes and using these same
knots for positioning is primarily an outgrowth of the rigging trades. Some earlier
users would have been found on sailing ships, in church steeple construction and
maintenance, in mines, and in tree-trimming trades.
Ropes and some type of body belt, for restraint or work-positioning support,
were particularly useful during stormy seas and above the decks of ships. A similar
development of harness, rope, and knot usage originated more recently from cliff
and cave rescue, as well as from mountaineering techniques. In the middle 1800s,
Introduction to Fall Protection • 9

The proper understanding of fall protection results in a commitment to
elimination of fall hazards, and this begins by recognizing fall hazards without
considering the risk. Let the insurance industry worry about the risk. By taking any
route, other than elimination of the hazard altogether, we keep the hazard alive.
Eliminating Fall Hazards
Eliminating fall hazards means finding a way to avoid the necessity of exposure to
heights. This is the number one goal of fall protection. If a hazard is eliminated,
then workers are not put at risk. For example, building a roof truss framework,
fully or partially at ground level, and lifting it into place, is better than assembling
it in the air while standing on the framing.
It’s true that all hazards cannot be eliminated from every particular situation.
However, by addressing the known hazards, we can predict how most of them
can be eliminated or reasonably controlled before workers are exposed to them.
A simple checklist is often all that’s needed because it forces visualization of how
the work is supposed to be done when completed correctly.
Also, simple products that effectively eliminate many fall hazards are available
on the market today. Some examples follow:
• A telescoping duster to remove cobwebs in the office or home. Basically
a dust mop on an extendable pole: this product allows a person to clean
ceilings, skylights, and stairwells without the use of a ladder.
• A fruit harvester. This product consists of a specially designed fruit-picking
basket that clamps onto any long pole. It eliminates fall hazards for workers
harvesting fruit from trees.
• Gutter cleaning device. This product consists of a sprayer that attaches to
a garden hose. An attached, extendable pole lifts the device to gutter level.
When the device is activated, high-pressure water blasts and lifts leaves and
debris from gutters, while the worker remains on the ground.
• Tank truck loading and unloading devices. Tank trucks that can be
loaded and unloaded by workers standing at ground level and eliminate fall
exposures for workers who would otherwise climb to the top of the tank
truck or trailer (Figure 1.13). Work from the ground, by design, requires
proper engineering and order by buyer of this model, for example vapor
recovery systems.
Are Fall Hazards Obvious?
Isn’t it obvious to any person (who may someday sit on a jury) that height hazards
are a known, severe-injury producer, if not a reasonably certain-fatality producer?
Then why don’t employers address this hazard exposure, which can be reasonably
eliminated or controlled? Why is such a severe and foreseeable hazard too often
Introduction to Fall Protection • 29

We can plan safety at heights, and we can train employees in better work
methods, but too many supervisors still leave the entire choice of work method
and safety provisions to the worker. “After all, he chose this line of work, and has
the job experience, so he should know best,” goes the reasoning, along with “I
can’t be with the worker, and do her job for her.”
Workers often play into this rationale by saying the boss said he will get me
anything I want for safety. While that is nice, the worker does not know what to
ask for, so the hazard exposures remain.
Too often, the necessary tools for safety have not been provided to the worker.
Tolerating fall hazards has become an unconsciously accepted practice many
managers develop early in their careers. The critical safety knowledge needed to
deal with heights safely is not inherent in the minds of most managers. It must be
learned. They unfortunately think that workers who fall were not careful enough
or simply were unlucky. “Poor Joe, what a shame,” is the refrain.
Prevention or Fall Arrest as a Means of Fall Protection?
Sometimes, exposure to a fall hazard cannot be practically prevented during access
to a work task or when at a work position, through such measures as floors, walls,
aerial lifts, bucket trucks, guardrails, perimeter cables, crane-suspended work
platforms (manbaskets), scaffolds, or planking. In these situations, personal fall
arrest equipment can be selected to control a fall or alternatively provide a reliable
means of escape when a controlled-descent feature is employed.
In general, personal protective equipment is designed as a backup safety system
for an individual during a work task. In the event of an emergency, the equipment
should function automatically to help protect the worker from harm. A personal-fall
protection system should, therefore, provide continuous and complete protection
without interfering with required task mobility. Continuous fall protection uses
one or more of the following means:
• Fall Prevention
Barriers, Covers
Guardrails
Perimeter Cables
Walls, Fences
Platforms, Buckets, Aerial Lifts
Scaffolds, Planking
• Fall Arrest
Safety Nets
Personal Fall Arrest Systems
Continuous or 100% fall protection means no gaps in fall protection coverage.
Many ask whether this can be done on an economical or practical basis. Properly
used, equipment can often provide the most protection for the least cost with a
certain level of potential exposure.

and exposure to publicity, have become very safety conscious. Surprisingly, they
have been successful in gaining the cooperation of building managers, sometimes
despite their bids being higher than their less safety-conscious competitors. The
result of this safety commitment is a vastly improved experience modification
rate, which pays back those safety-conscious owners in the best way of all—cash
savings!
According to data compiled by the B. G. Balmer Agency, Paoli, PA in 1992
and 1993, construction projects, insurance frequently represents 10 percent of
the price of the job. This means that if payroll is 40 percent of the job, then

Suitable ramp slopes, generally no greater than 1 in 12—with some relatively

Elevated Falls: Falls from One Level to Another
A momentary loss of balance resulting from a slip or trip can often lead to an
elevated fall. Grabbing onto something to catch oneself after balance is accidentally
lost is rare. For this reason, a handrail—or worse, a hand line—cannot be an
acceptable substitute for guardrails on either side of a leading edge.
Unlike many workplace hazards, few, if any, near-miss incidents help people
learn to appreciate the seriousness of elevated falls.
Close calls or near-misses that do not result in an incident (such as an automobile
cutting in front of you on the drive home, a slight slip on a wet floor, or a trip
on a stair) can serve to increase awareness that, in turn, generally leads to greater
caution. However, once a person loses his or her balance and falls from elevation,
whether it is 10 feet or 200 feet, serious or fatal injury usually results. In fact, the
worst elevated fall hazards are presented by the potential for sudden collapse or
walking into floor holes left after temporarily placed covers have been lifted and
lighting conditions are not the best.
In 1989, the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
issued a Hazard Alert to industry concerning the severe hazard resulting from
roof and floor openings, such as skylights or air-conditioning duct holes. All holes
and floor or roof openings must be either guarded or covered securely. Covers
must support the intended loads and be securely attached. They must be clearly
labeled with a warning, “OPENING: DO NOT REMOVE,” or the equivalent.
(See Figure 4.8). Concrete slabs and facades should have holes covered or plugged
before shipment from the manufacturer.
In 2004, a NIOSH Hazard Alert was issued on roof openings to highlight the
skylight hazard, and particularly the hazard of stepping or falling onto and through
nonstructural skylights. This was only the second time since 1971 that NIOSH
has repeated a Hazard Alert to notify employers and building owners of the dire
hazard of walking/working near skylights without a screen or railing protection
and especially due to degradation of the skylight material from ultraviolet
radiation.
Introduction to Fall Protection • 117

must be covered or guarded. If it is covered, the cover must meet the following
OSHA requirements:
• It must be secured adequately to prevent accidental displacement.
• It must be marked using a color-coding system or with the word “Hole” or
“Cover.” A proper warning system should be provided as directed by ANSI
Z535.4.
• It must support twice any anticipated load, which includes the weight of
employees, materials, and equipment (OSHA 1926.501(b)(4)).
Drywall or insulation boards, pallets, cardboard, roofing felt, thin plywood, or
other makeshift materials intended to keep noise or dust out must never be used
for roof or floor hole covers for any reason. They won’t support the weight of a
worker and can be easily displaced or collapse without warning. Holes subject to
weather or cold air must never be sealed with a black or clear plastic sheet such
as Visqueen because they are subject to displacement and fall through without
warning. All covers, including skylights, must be structurally designed to support a
falling worker from any angle.
During construction, when holes are, at times, unprotected (such as when
covers are being installed or removed) another form of fall protection must be
utilized, such as a net within a frame. A personal fall arrest system (PFAS) should
be used by the worker placing or removing the cover or a personnel net can be
placed beneath the hole. A net placed beneath the hole and left while the cover is
over the hole results in redundant protection, thereby increasing the safety factor.
However, if ducts, pipes, or other materials are being installed in the hole, a PFAS
should be used.
Skylights must also be protected. They often give workers and managers, including
real estate maintenance and inspection companies, a false sense of security; leaks
become the only consideration rather than the safety of the inspector. Skylights
are designed to resist the applicable environmental load requirements such as snow
loads, wind loads, live loads, and in some cases, hurricane-induced, windborne
debris impact loads. However, current U.S. design practices do not dictate that
they are to be manufactured to hold someone standing on them or dynamic loads
created when a person trips and falls against them. Most skylights are not designed
to hold a person’s weight even when they are new, and they become weaker and
more brittle with age. Many workers and teenagers on school roofs have fallen to
their deaths through skylights by merely stepping or sitting on them or leaning
against them. Slips and trips around unprotected skylights can also be lethal.
Unless unit skylights are screened, the glass, fiberglass, or plastic skylight domes
must be protected and the opening securely covered and marked or guardrails
installed. Protective screens (above) or grilles (underneath) are more frequently
used, especially after a fall-through. Screens must be capable of resisting a fall-
through sufficient to break the skylight. Grill-type screens and wired glass to
prevent intruder resistance must be engineered so as not to cut up a falling worker
upon impact.

A safety-monitor system is allowed on roofs 50 feet or less in width, without
a warning line, and where mechanical equipment is not being used or stored
[1926.502(g)(1)(iii)].
The employer must designate a competent person as a safety monitor, who
must be on the same roof and within visual sighting distance of the employees,
and must be close enough to verbally communicate with them; and the monitor
shall not have other responsibilities which could take the monitor’s attention away

Although OSHA does not provide for an hierarchy of protection, the author
believes that protection can reasonably be provided using a combination of
motion-stopping systems (barriers or fall arrest systems) and warning lines.
Can trained and hazard-knowledgeable monitors provide effective fall
protection? See Figure 8.8 and consider the following:
• According to University of Michigan research in the 1970s (Chaffin et. al
1978), and the author’s own field interviews, workers can fall from a standing
position over an edge within and beyond six feet by tripping, slipping,
stubbing, or loss of balance. In such situations, the monitor can not react
effectively to stop the fall over the edge by voice contact alone, once the fall
has started in that direction.
• How far from the edge should an employee be before being warned about
stepping over the edge? The minimum distance is 6 feet (1926.501(b)(10)).
This is the basis of the warning-line distance rule and keeps the worker’s
body on the roof. Since work inside this 6-foot limit is the basis of the
safety monitor’s role, if the trip or slip occurs, the monitor is powerless to
stop all falls. The author recommends 15 feet, optimally, for the warning line
and positive protection closer to the edge, or where a skylight or skylight
opening occurs.
• The monitor may become inattentive over a period of time. It is not
reasonable to expect continued, focused attention on one or more workers
near a roof edge. A monitor’s attention may easily be diverted for several
seconds, which is enough time to permit a worker to step over the edge. An
Introduction to Fall Protection • 333

Figure 8.8. Safety monitoring versus positive fall protection. A monitor’s shout
may be the last thing a worker hears as he or she hurtles to the ground. A
safety monitor is required for work between a warning line and the roof edge
unless fall arrest or other conventional fall protection is in place.
analogy can be drawn to a lifeguard who has to watch many swimmers, but
has difficulty tracking even one. Yet the lifeguard has only a few seconds to
react and reach a potential victim.
• Noise and other environmental conditions may distract the monitor over an
eight-hour day. Equipment and machinery noise in the area could obscure
warning sounds. If work starts early or finishes late, the light may diminish
and reduce visibility. Artificial lighting provides shadows, which permit some
fall hazards to go unnoticed.
• The monitor must warn the worker while the worker still retains control
over his or her balance, and before the worker inadvertently steps over an
edge. This should be before any worker is within one step (or 3 feet) away
from the edge, while moving backwards. Yet 50 percent of the time, inside
the warning line may be within the three-foot limit from a roof edge. A step
occurs at the rate of 3 feet per second, so one or two steps to the edge take
only one or two seconds.
• The worker must hear a warning. Use a call and response system where the
monitor must see the worker raise his or her hand to acknowledge hearing
334 • Fall Protection by Worker Activity

the warning. He or she could be deaf in one ear, have ears obscured by head
coverings, or could have a head cold. Also, the worker could be startled by
a machine starting up or be unaware of a warning because of background
noise.
• A warning from 50 feet away requires more time to be heard, than one given
from 10 feet away. Some roofing felts may extend over the edge without
being tacked or wrapped. This could lead to both the worker and monitor
being unaware of unstable footing. It could result in a step close to the edge
and an immediate fall over the edge. Even if both the monitor and worker
are aware of this, it’s an easy fact to forget momentarily. The eye can be
deceived when attention is diverted, even briefly.
• A worker’s reaction to spilled, hot roofing liquids may cause him or her
to step quickly to the side and possibly off or through the roof. This has
occurred in the author’s investigative experience, resulting in fatality in
one case.
• Raising material to the roof by a manual pulley system requires an employee
to be at the roof’s edge, looking down and communicating with a person
on the ground. The same situation is required to bring loads onto the roof.
If the load is upset or the pulley system tips, the employee may instinctively
grab the moving rope and can be pulled over the edge by the equipment.
In addition, the worker may reach for a load or may grab an unstable load
resulting in a loss of balance that can lead to a fall.
• A worker can lose balance due to one of the many possible distractions, such
as the following: stepping onto a slight depression or elevation (bubble) in
the roof; backing into an obstacle (e.g. pipe) behind the knee, experiencing
a trick knee, turning an ankle; spilling hot, liquid roofing material; inhaling
fumes; experiencing vibration; looking up momentarily into bright sunlight,
or watching a bird or plane overhead. Problems such as dizziness, sickness,
getting up suddenly, bending down rapidly, and then getting up and losing
grip on a load or object, may cause a fall, and probably beyond the control
of a monitor.
In past years, some roofing contractors have habitually appointed many or all
workers as safety monitors. The sight of safety monitors themselves engaged in
work close to roof edges with no other monitor watching them has been all too
common.
Many roofs of commercial buildings constructed since the 1950s have been
deficient in edge protection from fall hazards. It is occasionally necessary to approach
the edges of roofs for inspection, repair, equipment maintenance, re-roofing, or
for other reasons; in the course of these activities, significant hazards can occur
without the benefit of a building owner’s or manager’s plan to render the hazard
reasonably harmless. This situation is addressed in the ANSI Z359-2007 standard.
Where maintenance is known to be required, safe access should be addressed in the
architect’s plans for all parts of a building or structure under contract.

Measuring instruments have sensitivity represented in hertz (Hz). The force
transducer, which is used to measure maximum arresting force (MAF), can register
from 0.1 Hz to 10,000+ Hz. However, the test rig may interfere with test results
obtained as low as 250 Hz and produce spurious values, unless these undesirable
frequencies are filtered. In Britain, for many years, a 1,000-Hz sensitivity level was
chosen. But the human body is a much better energy absorber than a steel weight,
and the exact reproducibility of a drop is difficult, so the midheight of the wave
documented by the force transducer in a fall test was deemed the appropriate force
level.
Work done by Harry Crawford of the National Engineering Labs in Scotland
for the British Standards Institute has shown that a sensitivity of 100 Hz is a more
than adequate force measurement for personal fall devices.7 Ulysse and Sulowski
(1982) have shown that a steel test weight produces a force 20 percent to 50
percent higher than an anthropomorphic dummy does. And Chen Wang estimated
that steel weights create forces 50 percent to 100 percent higher than the human
body (Wang 1977). OSHA has adopted a 1.4:1 force factor of a steel weight to
the human body. In the United States, a maximum sensitivity level of 100–125 Hz
has been proposed, derived from a report to the ANSI Z359 committee by Jim
Brinkley of the Aerospace Medical Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air
Force Base. This recommendation is based upon ejection studies, cadaver skull
resonance, and related data (Brinkley et. al 1986).
At 100 or 125 Hz, the actual dynamic peak should be recorded when a fall
system’s arrest force is charted. (See the graphs in Figures 6.27 and 6.28 for the
measurement of MAF and force-test demonstrations, respectively). All resonance
due to the test rig and other unrelated peaks can then be eliminated or disregarded.

OSHA fall protection regulations for construction define the roles of fall
protection Competent Persons on construction sites. Competent persons may
perform different supervisory roles:
1. The Competent Person must have the authority to shut down the job if it
is not being done safely and according to the fall protection plan [OSHA
1926.502(k)].
2. The individual responsible for fall protection training must be a Competent
Person [1926.503 (a)(2)].
3. A Competent Person must periodically inspect fall protection equipment
and insure that employees know how to inspect their own equipment.
4. A safety monitor must be a Competent Person to warn others of roof edge
fall hazards within a controlled-access zone.
5. A fall protection plan must be implemented by a Competent Person.
These Competent Persons may be different persons who have different training
and different responsibilities.
The Competent Person must be provided with the proper authority, resources,
and assistance needed to perform his or her responsibilities. The Competent Person
should consult with and obtain information from authorized persons affected by the
facility fall protection program and procedures. This kind of feedback from the
users of the program is necessary for determining the success of the program and
the need for improvements or additions to the program.
It is not expected that a Competent Person will review site-standard fall
protection and rescue procedures each and every time work begins. However, the
Competent Person should review these procedures frequently enough to ensure
that the implementation of the program is correct and that authorized persons are
adequately informed about the fall protection and rescue procedures of the task
they are performing.
For nonstandard work at elevation, the Competent Person must be directly
involved in all aspects of planning, implementing, and monitoring the nonstandard
job.
Competent persons are encouraged to become Certified Safety Professionals
(www.bcsp.org) to add breadth to their qualifications.
The Qualified Person
Also presently required is the appointment of a Qualified Person, ideally a
representative of the structural or mechanical branch of engineering, to assist
in eliminating or controlling fall hazards at the design and planning stages of
each new construction and maintenance project. This Qualified Person must be
thoroughly familiar with state-of-the-art fall protection equipment and design
practices. Outside consultants may be employed to fill this roll at sites that do not
have qualified fall protection engineers.

Not everyone will be protected when some theoretical level of risk is deemed to be
acceptable by those involved in making financial decisions. Thus one group might
be willing to protect 50 percent of the weight range of an average population,
while others would see 95 percent as reasonable. Others would set a goal of
97 percent or 99 percent of the male population with a 1 lb. increase for each
year beyond a date of determination of that population. Still others would argue
that the chance of falling is very small because of vigilance of the individuals and
regular training on the nature of the hazards.
Instead of the word risk the word hazard should be used when communicating
with the workforce. Risk should be left to be used as a management and insurance
term; at best, it is a qualifier of the term hazard for safety professionals.
The author believes it is the duty of an organization, particularly its safety
professionals, to protect its entire exposed workforce against threats that could
cause loss of life by conducting proper and regular hazard assessments. Certainly
there is no 100 percent protection but the role of a safety professional is to protect
lives—reasonably all lives under his or her jurisdiction.
Note that several surveys may be needed to predict where workers may go
and what they may do, perhaps years later, that despite training, could give rise to
unexpected fall hazards. Also, make sure to identify fall hazards that might occur
under unusual conditions (e.g., a fan replacement, roof patch repair, turnaround
maintenance). When methods of fall protection might not work due to weather
conditions or missing components, acceptable alternatives are required as a backup
plan. If no acceptable solution is available, workers need to know that they can
stop work and seek assistance. The author’s policy is to have ready two means of
protection for each identified hazard. These procedures help maintain control.
Fall hazards involving outside contractors or visitors to a business (inspectors,
salespeople, or potential employees) should not be overlooked. Inspectors and
job estimators are provided an exemption by OSH, A but not by the civil courts
that examine through testimony whether fall hazards could reasonably have been
controlled or eliminated. Procedures for fall protection should be in place for
visitors, salespeople, delivery personnel, inspectors, field engineers, and architects.
Once a fall hazard is identified by an organization, it should not leave the open
or controlled list until it is generally agreed that it has been eliminated or addressed.
Identifying Hazardous Exposures
Fall-hazard analysis begins by listing the work tasks that involve or could involve
exposure to an elevated fall hazard. It is important to reemphasize that this should
include travel. For example, a valve that must be monitored regularly is located in
an elevated pipe rack and requires vertical and horizontal mobility for access and
egress, but the actual work task may be stationary. Other elevated work, such as
painting or sandblasting, may require more mobility.
Introduction to Fall Protection • 391

Tying It All Together
Down-to-earth facts show that fall protection provisions can reasonably be made
at the job-planning stage. Where the workers must go and what they must do is
known, so planning for them to do it safely seems obvious.
Too many owners and managers lump slip, trip, and fall hazards into one
category, and thus think about solutions in simple terms as well—“Watch your
step,” “Be careful,” “Take your time and don’t take chances.” These managers are
from the “Awareness School.” Unfortunately, this attitude does not translate into
employee hazard awareness or adequate training on how to properly address fall
hazards at elevation. Work can’t be done efficiently and productively without the
proper tools. Likewise, elevated fall protection can’t be accomplished without the
proper tools.
Selling the attitude of practical fall safety has never been simple, and the job is
never finished. Constant vigilance is the price paid to attain a zero-injury workplace.
This is a controllable cost that can yield remarkable dividends.
Incident Investigation
A comprehensive managed fall protection program should include requirements
for incident investigation in the event of accidental death, injury, or property
damage. To be effective, these investigations must be conducted promptly, with
well-established reporting procedures and documented results.
In the case of a fall or near-miss incident, the fall protection administrator should
appoint a competent or qualified person to conduct an incident investigation. The
investigation will help determine if the fall protection program has established
the appropriate control method for a given hazard, if the training is adequate, and
what improvements are needed to ensure such an incident does not reoccur.
Systems of root-cause analysis help identify the underlying causes of incidents
and are valuable for determining what corrective measures should be taken as a
result of the lessons learned. Many times, the result of an incident investigation
is that worker error is identified as the main contributing factor. When root-cause
analysis is used, multiple underlying causes are usually uncovered.
The fall protection program must be updated every time an investigation results
in a recommendation for improvement and whenever a new fall hazard is identified
or an existing hazard is modified.
Auditing and Program Evaluation
To continually improve any program, a means to gather feedback is important.
This can be achieved in a number of ways. Evaluation is necessary to check that the
elevated fall hazard control employed is working properly and is the most suitable
for the job. It can also serve as a means of addressing other safety problems at
the site.
406 • Managed Fall Protection Programs

Equipment Selection
Consider the following as a basis for selecting fall protection equipment.
Do you have a fall protection program? If so, will you choose what is necessary
rather than simply meeting the minimum state or federal requirements?
If you cringe when those questions come up, then you will probably make do
with harnesses and lanyards, regardless of the type of fall hazard.
The problem with selecting the minimum is that it costs employees their
productivity, and their feedback is exactly what can be expected—negative!
The problem with selecting the optimum is that it may be overkill and
unaffordable. A company may need several methods of fall protection that overlap,
with each method playing a vital part.
The question to ask is, “Are there any gaps in protection?” Fall protection must
be complete.
The primary selection method should be to apply the fall protection hierarchy
with rigor:
1. Elimination
2. Prevention
3. Restraint
4. Arrest
5. Administrative Controls, including: warning lines and training or controlled
access zones and safety monitoring
The search for fall hazard elimination begins during construction or renovation
with the architect/engineer in charge. No other professional can do this work. It
is incumbent upon the design professional to become aware of fall hazards so
that the hazards can be eliminated or controlled during construction, maintenance,
and demolition. In this context, elimination means that the design substitution or
sequence of work does not include fall hazards.
The search for fall prevention is also the domain of the architect/engineer. Fall
prevention is the use of permanent platforms and stairs for access, with suitable
guardrails. Some structures—light poles, for instance—call for temporary platform
access.
The selection of restraint or fall arrest equipment is a job the engineer usually
delegates to the general contractor, who then delegates to a subcontractor or,
alternatively, to the owner’s safety department. The knowledgeable engineer should
be available upon request to assist with anchorage-point design that will meet the
subcontractor’s anchorage-strength requirements. Otherwise, a fall protection
engineering consulting firm should be retained.
The quality of the fall arrest system begins with the properly fitted full-body
harness, to ensure subpelvic fall arrest and suspension comfort with minimum
waist or body discomfort. After careful analysis, other equipment must be selected
based upon the work.1
416 • Equipment Selection, Inspection, and Maintenance

scope of protection across various job phases. Then the manager may be able
to show that he or she has looked at the work carefully, examined failure modes,
and matched usable and acceptable fall protection systems to that particular work,
without relying solely on the individual worker’s judgment or experience. Over
time, managerial diligence will result in a record that shows the methods of fall
protection employed have been appropriate and that workers have been educated
to use well-thought-out systems for personal protection.
What’s Wrong with Present Methods of Fall Protection?
Many employers regard fall hazards as a necessary occupational risk and overlook
them, depending instead on workers’ practical ability.
The typical philosophy has been to encourage workers exposed to fall hazards
to tie off when stationary or when working. However, the choice is usually left
up to the workers or, as workers often refer to it, on-the-job training (OJT). In
this case, the risk factors for injury are overlooked, and the standards are never
consulted.
If general practice encourages tie-off, a legitimate question arises: What’s wrong
with tying off? The answer is as follows:
1. By definition, it means that a worker is unprotected and exposed to a fall
both before and after tying off.
2. It means that untested, understrength anchorage points may be used and
that the workers must judge the strength of any object.
3. It invariably means that the fall protection equipment must be wrapped
around a structural member and then attached back to itself—a method
rejected by fall equipment manufacturers, and one that also restricts mobility.
4. It encourages the use of knots in rope lifelines and lanyards as a means
of securing, but in actuality, bend knots can considerably reduce the rope’s
strength.
5. It means that the shape, sharpness, and contour of the tie-off points can
set up a cutting action, which can be instantaneous and catastrophic in some
falls. The warning provided by the Canadian Standards Association Fall
Protection Committee in 1987, recreated in the sidebar page 92, points to an
urgent need for radical rethinking of this concept.
Introduction to Fall Protection • 91

Allowing an untrained employee to use fall arrest equipment is like allowing an
untrained driver to operate a motor vehicle. Not only is the untrained employee at
great risk, he or she also jeopardizes the safety of his or her coworkers. Properly
trained employees using the proper fall protection equipment are an essential
element of any fall protection program. This chapter provides insight on training
workers, supervisors, engineers, and administrators on how to conduct and manage
work at elevation.
Training Program Basics
The need for training cannot be overemphasized! It is the first step toward increasing
awareness and developing an understanding of the capabilities and limitations
of available equipment. Initial training of the safety committee by a competent
person is needed to ensure that the fall hazard analysis is properly performed.
Then, supervisors or lead persons can be trained as competent persons, receiving
instruction in fall protection principles, techniques, and equipment performance.
The “training of the trainers” forms the basis of an in-house team that can provide
live practice sessions. Ongoing training is as critical as the initial overview. Periodic
refresher instruction for competent person trainers and authorized persons,
who are the end-users of fall protection procedures and equipment, can serve
to reinforce proper equipment use and care, as well as provide an opportunity to
review new technology. Training is the key to making workers aware of danger
and advising them on how to attach and use the proper equipment once anchor
points have been selected. Technical knowledge, site-specific information, hands-
on demonstrations, and work experience are all necessary for a successful fall
protection training program.
Whenever active fall protection systems are used in the workplace, training must
be provided to workers, supervisors, and others whose responsibilities expose
them to fall hazards or require them to supervise those exposed to fall hazards.
Generally, he further up the chosen fall protection method is on the fall protection
heirarchy of controls, the more training is required (see Figure 11.1).
Workers learn from training both in a classroom environment and through on-
the-job experiences. They learn through classroom exercises and properly executed
field repetition to advance their knowledge. They must also learn to integrate what
they learn with future work situations that might be very different from their
training. The best instruction methods for workers provide training that is relevant
to industry-specific and site-specific work. This type of training is sometimes the
hardest to develop and provide.
Workers need training to understand the rules and how they apply in real life
situations. They frequently are simply unaware of dangerous situations such as
equipment compatibility problems, the consequences of a sudden free fall or the
possibility of impact with a stationary object. Workers must be trained that safety
is their responsibility and that taking the time to do a job properly is the safest way
to protect themselves and their coworkers. To achieve this, training must provide
438 • Fall Protection Training

• able to approve fall protection and rescue equipment and systems;
• a representative on employer’s primary or leadership safety committee and
able to select and appoint fall protection safety committee personnel;
• able to identify when it is necessary to involve a Qualified Person in fall
protection for designing, installing, and maintaining the employer’s fall
protection systems; and
• able to lead fall protection accident and incident investigations and be
responsible for issuing written reports.
Program administrators may find that a survey by a qualified fall protection
consultant can open new insight by helping to identify fall protection concerns
they and their teams have inadvertently overlooked.
Employers should encourage local union shops to train and certify
Competent Persons, Competent Person Trainers and Authorized Persons.
Workers should get firsthand experience or at least watch a live training session
before being tested.
How Should Instruction Be Given?
In all cases, fall arrest equipment is designed for people, and therefore people
should have the opportunity to practice with their personal protective equipment
to learn its capabilities and limitations. The objective of training is to determine
what additional skill, knowledge, or understanding an individual or group needs
to perform their responsibilities with maximum efficiency and effectiveness and
without incidents. An understanding of the equipment and its limitations enables
employees to work out simple sequences of moving with protection. Product
warnings and instructions should be carefully read. Firsthand experience in a live
classroom situation, as shown in Figure 11.3, or on-site is invaluable in a well-
organized program.
Historically, and for obvious reasons, fall protection training with a 6-foot lanyard
and harness has been limited to equipment inspection and relating a few points on
tying off when stationary. Training without experience is much like trying to teach
a person to swim without entering the water. This is particularly important with
life-protecting personal equipment. Consider the amount of performance training
done with respiratory protective equipment. Why should fall arrest equipment be
an exception?
Today’s personal fall arrest systems now have low arresting force levels and
are manufactured with comfort of the user in mind. These systems can provide
an opportunity to personally try out arrest protection equipment in a supervised
training session with minimal risk of injury. A trainee does not have to experience
a fall in equipment; merely donning a harness and being suspended from a tripod
or other suitable anchor point will allow the user to understand how to properly fit
a harness, how the equipment will feel on the body in the event of a fall, and how
to move the lags or use safety devices to prevent suspension trauma after a fall.
Introduction to Fall Protection • 447

The Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA) has joint Labor/
Management Funds that focus on safety and health along with skills training. The
Laborers have over 70 training centers throughout North America that conduct
safety and skills training and fall protection training is an essential part of their
curriculum.
The United Brotherhood of Carpenters (UBC) has over 200 training centers in
the United States and has a keen interest in fall protection training.
The United Auto Workers Union (UAW) has contributed greatly to controlling
fall hazards at automobile plants in recent years by a willingness to research the
solutions, write procedures, and train the workforce using company funds. The
unions will play a special role in abatement of fall hazards at the work site in the
years ahead; there is nothing wrong in safety for safety’s sake.
Behavior-based safety programs can help organizations to reorganize, identify,
and document potential fall hazards, but this can only be successful if management
lives up to a commitment to eliminate or counter those fall hazards within a
reasonable time period. Sometimes these types of programs can lead to a blame-
the-worker mentality and encourage lack of reporting by the workers. Therefore,
the design of a behavior-based program is crucial and should emphasize safety, not
lack of reporting. Remember that our goal is intended to be the steady elimination
of hazards through design-based safety.
Summary
Training is a necessary element of every fall protection plan and program.
Remember that sufficient time is required for a training course to be effective. For
example a one day tower training course may be insufficient, but a classroom day
combined with a field day may be appropriate for Authorized Persons. Engineers,
managers, supervisors, and workers can be expected to operate safely only after
they have been trained in industry-acceptable operations, practices, and guidelines.
People who have not been given the proper equipment and properly trained can
expect to get injured and possibly even killed.
Training must also be accompanied by field observations for unsafe acts and
unsafe conditions, supervisory enforcement of safety rules and guidelines, and
periodic retraining to keep everyone aware of expected operating culture.
ANSI/ASSE Z359.2 - 2007 Minimum Requirements for a Comprehensive Managed Fall
Protection Program establishes guidelines and requirements for an employer’s managed
fall protection program, including policies, duties, and training; fall protection
procedures; eliminating and controlling fall hazards; rescue procedures; incident
investigations; and evaluating program effectiveness. ANSI/ASSE Z490.1 –
2001 Criteria for Accepted Practices in Safety, Health and Environmental Training includes
information on training program development, delivery, evaluation, and program
management. The purpose of this standard is to provide accepted general practices
for all safety, health, and environmental training. All fall protection trainers and
program administrators should be familiar with this standard.

than in the nonforested areas that replace them. Additionally, tropical rain forests
occupy less than 7% of the land surface but contain more than half of all plant and

adjacent deforested areas.30 This boundary zone has greater exposure to winds, easier
access by livestock and humans, and many other effects that result in a loss of plant
and animal species at the edge. Edge effects greatly magnify the adverse effects of
deforested areas.
The Brazilian Amazon is the largest region of tropical forest in the world,
containing 31% of the world’s total.30 NASA’s (National Aeronautics and Space

natural disasters in U.S. history. By August 30, 2005, one day after the category 3

patterns are established, and how much moisture is deposited. Temperature and
